newsitem.title: BELGIUM: OLYMPICS-EPO TEST READY BUT NEEDS LEGAL MUSCLE.
newsitem.headline: OLYMPICS-EPO TEST READY BUT NEEDS LEGAL MUSCLE.

text.p: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) has finalised its test to detect the dangerous drug erythropoietin (EPO) but is delaying its introduction to ensure it can withstand legal scrutiny, IOC member Jacques Rogge said on Friday.
"The test is ready, EPO can be traced but we still need to cover ourselves better legally," Rogge told the Belgian Het Nieuwsblad newspaper in an interview.
Rogge, who is also chairman of the federation of European National Olympic Committees, said "the door will certainly be closed" for EPO users at the 2000 Olympic Games in Sydney.

EPO, which stimulates the production of red blood cells which transport oxygen around the body, is considered one of the most dangerous drugs. Extended use can thicken the blood and cause heart attacks, studies have shown.
Belgian Rogge said there was also a 50 percent chance that the human growth hormone, seen as the ideal substitute for steroids, could be traced by Sydney 2000.
Rogge, seen as a potential successor to IOC president Juan-Antonio Samaranch, said the IOC knew of the existence of EPO in 1987.
He also said he has realised that the war against doping could never be won. "But it is our duty to keep disease at the lowest possible minimum," he said.
"Even if I have to admit that regarding EPO and growth hormone we have incurred a big backlog, I remain optimistic."
He said the lab test for EPO had been tried out and was watertight for white athletes.
But tests for black and Asian athletes are still in progress and are due to be completed by next year, he said.
"It's a pity we are losing time but it is necessary. Otherwise each court would question the scientific value (of the test)," he said.
A faltering legal basis already hampered the IOC at the 1996 Games in Atlanta after seven athletes were caught using the substance Bromantan and were disqualified.

"The arbitration committee judged that there was not enough evidence that it was a stimulant. Two months later we had (that proof) but athletes were acquitted because we had to play it all legally correct," he said.
Rogge also urged another, more preventive approach in the fight against drug taking in sports.
"We know via informers that other products are already on their way and will be ready for commercial use only in three or five years," Rogge said.

"So let us work in a different way, investigate production (of substances) and find out what could have an influence on performance and health. Such studies certainly take five years. But if we work preventively, we could be ready with a test when the product really enters the market," he said.
